verses.text: Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father. Treat younger men as brothers,
older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity.
Honor the widows who are truly widows.
But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.
The widow who is truly in need and left all alone puts her hope in God and continues night and day in her petitions and prayers.
But she who lives for pleasure is dead even while she is still alive.
Give these instructions to the believers, so that they will be above reproach.
If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
A widow should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, the wife of one man,
and well known for good deeds such as bringing up children, entertaining strangers, washing the feet of the saints, imparting relief to the afflicted, and devoting herself to every good work.
But refuse to enroll younger widows. For when their passions draw them away from Christ, they will want to marry,
and thus will incur judgment because they are setting aside their first faith.
At the same time they will also learn to be idle, going from house to house and being not only idle, but also gossips and busybodies, discussing things they should not mention.
So I advise the younger widows to marry, have children, and manage their households, denying the adversary occasion for slander.
For some have already turned aside to follow Satan.
If any believing woman has dependent widows, she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened, so that it can help the widows who are truly in need.
Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching.
For the Scripture says, "Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain," and, "The worker is worthy of his wages."
Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses.
But those who persist in sin should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin.
I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels to maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality.
Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.
Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments.
The sins of some men are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others do not surface until later.
In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden.

context.author: Paul the apostle (1:1), though some scholars question this
context.genre: Pastoral letter, personal advice from a mentor
context.audience: Timothy, Paul’s younger coworker, left in Ephesus
context.mapLabel: EPHESUS, CARE IN THE CHURCH FAMILY
context.setting: Paul tells Timothy how to treat different groups in the church: older men and women as parents, younger as siblings. He gives detailed instructions for widows, since the church supported those without family, and for elders who deserve double honor and must not be accused lightly.
context.custom: There was no social safety net, and a widow without family was in danger. The church kept a list of widows over sixty who had been faithful. Younger widows were encouraged to remarry. Elders who worked hard in teaching were paid.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 6 completes the letter with slaves, false teachers, and money.
context.timelineBible: “Do not muzzle an ox” (v.18) quotes Deuteronomy 25:4. “The laborer deserves his wages” echoes Jesus (Luke 10:7). Two or three witnesses (v.19) comes from Deuteronomy 19:15.
context.sparkNotes: Treat older men as fathers and younger as brothers, older women as mothers, younger as sisters. Honor widows who are truly widows. A family should care for its own, and anyone who does not provide for relatives has denied the faith. Elders who rule well are worthy of double honor. Do not accept an accusation against an elder except on two or three witnesses. Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands.

translation.meaning: Honor and pay. Honor can mean financial support, as in “honor your father and mother.”
A widow truly alone, with no family to rely on.

Do not mistreat any widow or orphan.

overview.summary: The church is a family. Paul gives guidance on caring for widows, honoring and protecting elders, and being careful in choosing leaders.
overview.settingLine: Paul writes to Timothy, who is working in Ephesus.

history.t: A widow in the ancient Mediterranean world often had no income of her own and depended on her family. The Old Testament names widows, orphans and foreigners as those God protects (Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:19-21), and Acts 6:1 says widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution at Jerusalem. In 1 Timothy 5 the family is responsible first, then the church.

Paul says elders who lead well are worthy of "double honor" (5:17). The word for honor was also used for payment, and in 5:18 he cites Deuteronomy 25:4 about the ox and a saying about workers deserving their wages (compare Luke 10:7). That fits support. Whether "double" means twice the pay, twice the respect or simply generous honor is unclear.

customs.t: No widow is to be "enrolled" unless she is at least sixty, "the wife of one husband," and known for good works (5:9-10). The letter does not say what the list was for. It may have been a roll of widows receiving support, a group with a service role, or both. Scholars differ. Younger widows are told to marry (5:11-14).

Paul tells Timothy to "stop drinking only water" and to use "a little wine" for his stomach and frequent illnesses (5:23). Wine was an ordinary drink, usually mixed with water, and ancient doctors prescribed it for stomach complaints. The verse is a personal note that sits between lines on purity (5:22) and on sins that are plain or hidden (5:24-25).

archaeology.t: Greek and Latin epitaphs praise women who stayed with one husband. The Latin word is univira, "a one-man woman." The phrase in 5:9, "the wife of one husband," sounds like this kind of praise, though many surviving examples are later than Paul and from Rome.

City inscriptions in Asia Minor honor wealthy donors for gifts of money, grain, oil and public feasts. Scholars note that such gifts usually went to the city or its citizens as a whole, not to the poor as a class, which makes the church's care for its widows (5:3-16) stand out. This is a general picture, not a record from Ephesus.

overview.discussion: Paul calls the church a family. Who is a member of my church or neighborhood that I could care for the way I would a relative?
overview.book: The first letter to Timothy · 6 chapters. A mentor’s guide to leading a church well.
overview.author: Paul

historicalImage.caption: The Prophetess Anna, by Rembrandt (17th century). Luke 2:36-37 describes Anna, an elderly widow who stayed in the temple worshiping night and day. First Timothy 5:5 describes a widow left alone who sets her hope on God and continues night and day in prayer.

currentImage.caption: A statue of Plancia Magna, a wealthy woman of Perge who paid for public buildings in the 2nd century AD, in the Antalya Museum. Perge is not Ephesus and she lived after Paul, but she shows that women in the cities of Asia Minor could hold civic honors and fund public works. That is part of the background scholars raise for 1 Timothy 2:9-10 and 5:10.
